text: Fair. You're right, I did that. My own bias: I like the boring box. I like that politicians here can lose an election and still have a beer together. I've never been sure if that's maturity or just a nicer way of not saying what you think.

speaker: Host
text: Let me bring us back to Utah, because there's one moment in the reactions that doesn't fit any of our theories. At the memorial, Kirk's widow, Erika Kirk, publicly forgave the killer. In a stadium. Is forgiveness politically possible for either of your sides? Or only in private?

speaker: Guest
text: It's a private virtue, Carter. It's beautiful in a church. In politics, you don't forgive an aggressor who's still trying to take apart your home. You resist him. Forgiving in politics is just surrender in a nicer coat.

speaker: Guest2
text: Spoken like a man who's never had to forgive anyone in public. I've sat in rooms with families after a police shooting, and nobody there thinks forgiveness is surrender. Sometimes it's the only power you have left. You don't forgive for the killer. You forgive so the killer doesn't get to own the rest of your life.

speaker: Guest
text: That's a fair hit, and I don't like it. But you're describing grief, Clara, not politics. A family can forgive. A state that forgives everything stops being a state.

speaker: Host
text: Even your Schmitt doesn't quite say that. In the later foreword: 'The big problem is the limitation of war,' and limiting it is 'a cynical game, the organization of a dog fight, or an empty self-deception, unless it is connected on both sides with a relativization of the enmity.' Relativising the enmity, Elliot. Isn't that what forgiveness looks like in politics?

speaker: Guest
text: That's a dirty trick, using my own author.

speaker: Host
text: I learned it from Clara. Twenty minutes ago.

speaker: Guest2
text: I'll take that. And I'll say something I didn't expect to say. I don't think she was being naive. I think it was the most political thing anybody did that whole month. It cost her something, and it refused the script everyone else was reading from.

speaker: Host
text: Okay. Last question on my card, and I want real answers. Who in your own life do you no longer talk to because of politics? And do you miss them?

speaker: Guest2
text: Can I say something first? Something that isn't an answer to the question?

speaker: Host
text: Go on.

speaker: Guest2
text: About ten years ago I wrote a book. Short, angry, very popular in certain bookshops. It was about naming the enemy, basically, about how the left had to stop being nice and draw a hard line. And it sold, and people quoted it at demonstrations, and I was proud of it. And my oldest friend from school, a nurse, very ordinary, votes for whoever promises to fix the hospital, read it and asked me if she was on the other side of my line. Because she'd voted for a party I named in chapter three. I told her it wasn't about people like her. And she said, 'Clara, it's always about people like me.' We haven't really spoken since.

speaker: Host
text: Wow. That's... yeah.

speaker: Guest2
text: I half regret that book. Half. The analysis was right. The tone told people like her that they weren't wanted. And that's how you lose.

speaker: Guest
text: [sighs] That's... I'm sorry, Clara. I mean it. That's a real loss.

speaker: Guest2
text: Thank you.

speaker: Guest
text: Though I'd love to know which party was in chapter three.

speaker: Guest2
text: [laughs] Of course you would.

speaker: Host
text: Elliot. Your turn. Who?

speaker: Guest
text: My brother. Younger brother. He lives in Aarhus, teaches at a gymnasium, a decent man. After my institute business he wrote me a long email saying he couldn't defend me any more, that my ideas made him afraid for his students. We haven't spoken in five years. My daughter sees his children at Christmas. I don't go.

speaker: Host
text: Do you miss him?

speaker: Guest
text: Every Christmas. Next question.

speaker: Host
text: No next question. I want to stay here a second. My honest view: all the Schmitt and the Mouffe and the spreadsheets of the dead, that's not the real war. The real war is the Christmas you don't go to. The friend from school asking if she's on the other side of the line. That's where it's being fought, and both of you are losing it.

speaker: Guest2
text: That's not fair.

speaker: Host
text: Maybe not. But I don't think it's wrong either.

speaker: Guest
text: It's fair. I don't like it, but it's fair. And I'll tell you what frightens me, Carter, since we're being honest. It isn't Clara. It's the twenty-year-olds on both sides who've never had a brother to lose, because they grew up already sorted. My daughter's friends don't know a single person who votes the other way. When that generation runs the country, there won't be a Christmas left to skip.

speaker: Host
text: Right. So what do we take home? Five points, my view, not a peace treaty. One: it's not a war yet. Kalmoe and Mason are clear that the violence is nothing like the American past. But the vocabulary of war is spreading much faster than the violence, and words go first.

speaker: Host
text: Two: the anger is running ahead of the disagreement. Mason's line, we act like we disagree more than we really do. Today proved it the other way round as well: when these two actually talked about wages and housing, they disagreed less than when they talked about each other.

speaker: Host
text: Three: the reactions told us more than the crime did. We still don't know, legally, why Charlie Kirk was killed. But we know exactly how everybody behaved afterwards: the celebrations, the lists, the firings, the regulator going after a comedian. Everyone discovered they hate the machine only when it's pointed at their own people.

speaker: Host
text: Four: leaders matter. In Kalmoe and Mason's tests, anti-violence messages from both a Democratic and a Republican leader actually reduced support for partisan violence. So when a leader chooses blame over calm, that's a choice, and it has a cost.

speaker: Host
text: And five: you can fight like hell and still call the other side adversaries. That's Mouffe's whole point, and in his own way even Schmitt's. If we lose the difference between adversary and enemy, we lose the thing that lets us lose an election and go home alive. Elliot, a closing line.

speaker: Guest
text: Call them adversaries if it helps you sleep, Carter. But a people that can't name its enemy will eventually be named by them. I'd rather be honest and lonely than polite and gone.

speaker: Host
text: Clara.

speaker: Guest2
text: I hope we don't wake up one day having lost the cousins, the friends, the brothers, and only then call it the first shot, when it was really the thousandth.

speaker: Host
text: Thank you both. That was honest, and it hurt, which is probably how it should feel. A reminder: Tyler Robinson is the accused, he has pleaded not guilty, and no court has established why Charlie Kirk was killed. Our guests' views are their own, and every source is in the show notes. Next time on Fault Lines, another crack in the ground. I'm Carter. Go and ring someone you've stopped talking to. Or at least think about it.
